profile.reading: This OpenStreetMap record is one of eleven adjacent building footprints in Compass Datacenters Red Oak development, a wholesale data center campus in Ellis County, Texas, just south of the Dallas-Fort Worth core. This particular footprint sits in the westernmost row of the campus, the middle building of five arranged along that row. Compass Datacenters own market materials describe this campus, part of its Dallas-Fort Worth market, as a 360 megawatt development that was still nearing completion as of the most recent site content reviewed, with a confirmed 200 million dollar expansion phase announced in April 2024 that added two buildings totaling more than 500,000 square feet. A separate July 2026 company news item states that Red Oak now hosts seven data centers total, though that figure appears to describe the city of Red Oak as a whole rather than Compass own building count specifically, so it should not be read as confirming exactly how many of the eleven OpenStreetMap footprints in this cluster are Compass-operated versus operated by other companies also active in the area. Compass Datacenters was founded in 2011 by Chris Crosby, a former Digital Realty senior executive who remains the company CEO, and completed its first data center, a 1.2 megawatt facility, in 2012. The company is headquartered in Dallas, Texas, and describes its current ownership, per its own about-us page, as Ontario Teachers Pension Plan, RedBird Capital Partners, and company management. Beyond Dallas-Fort Worth, Compass 2026 markets list includes active developments in Chicago Hoffman Estates, Northern Virginia Loudoun County, Toronto, and Milan, plus a newly broken-ground site in Meridian, Mississippi, alongside earlier markets including Minneapolis and Nashville that the company has since exited or transferred to independent ownership. Separately, Compass donated 12.6 million dollars to fund a 40,000 square foot workforce-training replica data center at 300 Houston School Road in Red Oak, operated by Texas State Technical College, a distinct facility from the wholesale buildings mapped here that should not be confused with them. No per-building capacity, square footage, tenant, or year-built figure could be confirmed for this specific structure within the campus, and no local government permit or tax-abatement record could be retrieved this session, so those figures are deliberately omitted rather than estimated from the campus-wide totals above.

reading.body:
Compass Datacenters' Red Oak campus in Ellis County, Texas is a wholesale development south of Dallas-Fort Worth that the operator describes as targeting 360 megawatts at full buildout. This facility record identifies one of at least ten buildings in the cluster mapped on OpenStreetMap, positioned in the westernmost row of the campus. No individual building capacity, square footage, or tenant information has been published by the operator, so the scale and current operational status of this specific structure cannot be determined from available sources.

The Red Oak campus received a confirmed 200 million dollar expansion in April 2024 adding two buildings totaling over 500,000 square feet, indicating active development as of that date. The operator's most recent available materials describe the campus as still nearing completion, though a July 2026 news item references seven data centers in Red Oak without specifying whether all operate under Compass or whether other operators also occupy footprints in this cluster. The campus overall remains unranked among Texas facilities with published capacity figures because no current megawatt total has been attributed to it in operator materials this site could confirm.

At the state level, Texas has 133 mapped data center facilities and only 18 with published megawatt figures totaling 468 megawatts. Red Oak's exclusion from published capacity rankings reflects a pattern across most Texas facilities, which do not disclose power specifications publicly. Without confirmed figures for either this building or its campus, the site cannot yet quantify its role in Texas' or the grid's constraints on AI scaling.
